sentences.text: Galahadosuchus was a gracile, extinct saltoposuchid crocodylomorph characterized by long, slender limbs.
The known remains include a partial postcranial skeleton with most hindlimbs, an almost complete forelimb, tail vertebrae, isolated osteoderms, ribs, and the remains of a rhynchocephalian reptile.

Distinguishing features include relatively short and stout ulnare and radiale proximal carpal bones, which exceed a quarter of their maximum length but are at most one-tenth the length of their respective paired limb bones in the forearm.
The back of Galahadosuchus was covered by a double row of paramedian osteoderms, similar to other early crocodylomorphs.
The holotype specimen was recovered by Ron Croucher in 1969 at site 1 of the fissure deposits at Cromhall Quarry in Gloucestershire, southwest England.
The only known species of Galahadosuchus is G. jonesi, a new genus and species named Galahadosuchus jonesi.
Galahadosuchus is considered a terrestrial quadruped with an erect, digitigrade stance adapted for a fast-running lifestyle.
The fifth metacarpal of Galahadosuchus was less developed than in Terrestrisuchus and resembled the first digit.
The interpretation that the shortened first digit did not bear weight in Galahadosuchus is based on the shortened first metacarpal.
Galahadosuchus is classified as a member of the order Crocodylomorpha and the family Saltoposuchidae, and is classified within the clade Saltoposuchidae as the sister taxon to Terrestrisuchus.
Phylogenetic analyses found Galahadosuchus to be the sister taxon of Terrestrisuchus.
Galahadosuchus lived during the Late Triassic, specifically the Carnian to Rhaetian stages, in the Late Triassic fissure deposits of the Bristol Channel area in southwest England and south Wales.
It is debated whether different weighting methods in phylogenetic analysis affect the placement of Galahadosuchus within the family Saltoposuchidae.
Researchers debate whether the humerus proportions indicate Galahadosuchus was less capable of terrestrial movement, noting potential dataset biases from including modern crocodiles.
